title: Blue Hour and Interior
premise: Mirabel Okafor has spent twelve years mailing postcards to a house that burned down, writing to his brother Emeka, who died in the fire the night of an argument Mirabel can't stop replaying. When he hears their unfinished song playing on the radio—recorded by someone who shouldn't have it—he realizes Emeka survived long enough to send it into the world, and that the family's careful silence about that night was arranged to protect him, not themselves. Following the song's trail forces him home to confront his mother, who orchestrated the silence, and the truth: Emeka left the fire alive, chose not to come back, and died years later under another name. In the end, Mirabel writes one last postcard—not to the burned address but to the living woman Emeka loved—and finally says the thing whole.
about_author: Marguerite Voss is the pen name of a former court stenographer who spent two decades transcribing other people's confessions before writing her own fictions. She lives in a coastal town where she still writes letters by hand, most of them never sent.

chapters.title: The Address That Isn't
chapters.summary: Mirabel, in third person limited, buys postcards at a stationery shop and mails one to a lot where nothing stands. We learn the ritual: every month for twelve years, a few almost-true sentences. Emotional beat: tenderness disguised as routine.

chapters.title: A Song Out of Order
chapters.summary: In his car outside work, Mirabel hears a melody on a late-night radio program—the bridge of a song only he and Emeka ever knew, never recorded. The DJ credits a composer named 'E. Oka.' POV: Mirabel. Beat: the floor of his ordered life gives way.

chapters.title: Inventory of Almosts
chapters.summary: Mirabel rereads twelve years of unsent drafts kept in a shoebox, cataloguing everything he nearly said. Flashbacks establish the argument the night of the fire. POV: Mirabel with brief italicized letter interludes. Beat: grief as an archive.

chapters.title: The Mother Who Answers Questions With Tea
chapters.summary: He calls his mother, Adaeze, probing about the song; she deflects with talk of weather and cousins. He notices she doesn't ask what song. POV: Mirabel. Beat: suspicion arriving like cold air under a door.

chapters.title: What the Fire Report Didn't Say
chapters.summary: Mirabel requests the old fire report and finds a discrepancy: the remains identified were incomplete, and a neighbor's statement was withdrawn. POV: alternating Mirabel and a retired investigator, Ruth Calloway, via her journal. Beat: the first hard fact.

chapters.title: Ruth Keeps Her Own Files
chapters.summary: Ruth, now seventy, admits she never closed the case because the evidence didn't fit the story everyone wanted. She warns him: some families build houses on silences. POV: Ruth. Beat: reluctant alliance.

chapters.title: The Cousin Who Signed Nothing
chapters.summary: Mirabel tracks down cousin Chidi, who handled the funeral arrangements, and catches him in a small lie about who identified the body. POV: Mirabel. Beat: loyalty beginning to feel like complicity.

chapters.title: Postcard, Returned
chapters.summary: One of Mirabel's old postcards comes back stamped 'addressee unknown'—but postmarked from a city three hundred miles away, dated last spring. Someone has been receiving them. POV: Mirabel. Beat: vertigo; the dead may be a forwarding address.

chapters.title: Adaeze Breaks a Cup
chapters.summary: Mirabel visits unannounced; when he mentions the returned postmark, his mother shatters a teacup and says, 'You want to be right or you want to be family?' POV: Adaeze, first time in her head. Beat: the wall shows its architecture.

chapters.title: The Woman in the Photograph
chapters.summary: Among Emeka's things, Mirabel finds a photo of a woman, June Abara, torn but kept. Ruth finds a June Abara living near the postmark city. POV: Ruth. Beat: hope sharpening into dread.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Forwarding
chapters.summary: It emerges that Adaeze paid a postal clerk for years to forward Mirabel's postcards to an unknown destination—and to report back if any reply came. None did. POV: Adaeze. Beat: love as surveillance; the mother's guilt made concrete.

chapters.title: The Song's Second Verse
chapters.summary: The radio program airs again; the DJ reveals 'E. Oka' mailed the recording to the station eleven years ago with no return address. Mirabel drives toward the city. POV: Mirabel. Beat: pilgrimage begun.

chapters.title: June Answers the Door
chapters.summary: June Abara, wary, recognizes Mirabel's face before his name. She confirms she knew Emeka—under another name—in his final years. POV: June. Beat: the past opening like a door off its hinges.

chapters.title: The Name He Chose
chapters.summary: June tells of 'Emmanuel Okon,' a gentle man who played piano at a community center, who said his family thought he was dead and asked her never to correct them. POV: June. Beat: grief complicated by anger—Emeka chose absence.

chapters.title: Why He Walked Away
chapters.summary: Through June's account and Ruth's files, the truth assembles: the fire started during the argument; Emeka fled believing he'd caused a death; the incomplete remains belonged to a squatter. He couldn't return to a family built on his supposed corpse. POV: alternating June and Mirabel. Beat: justice outside the law—no crime, only damage.

chapters.title: Emmanuel Dies on a Tuesday
chapters.summary: June recounts his quiet death nine years ago, and how she honored his wish: no notice sent home. But she kept the postcards he secretly received and read, never answered. POV: June. Beat: the cruelest mercy—he heard his brother all along.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Burned Lot
chapters.summary: Mirabel brings Adaeze to the empty address. The family's arrangement collapses into accusation and confession: each protected the others from a truth none could survive saying. POV: Mirabel and Adaeze in counterpoint. Beat: climax—loyalty and truth tearing the same wound.

chapters.title: What the Postcards Were For
chapters.summary: Adaeze admits she forwarded them so Emeka would know he was forgiven without having to earn it. Mirabel understands his twelve years of almost-saying were answered every month. POV: Adaeze. Beat: devastation transfigured into terrible grace.

chapters.title: Reading the Unanswered
chapters.summary: June gives Mirabel the box: forty postcards, edges soft from handling. On the last one, faint pencil marks—a begun reply, never finished. POV: Mirabel. Beat: mourning finally given its object.

chapters.title: The Last Verse Said Whole
chapters.summary: At the community center piano, Mirabel plays the song through to the ending he and Emeka never wrote, and speaks aloud the apology and the accusation together. POV: Mirabel. Beat: identity reclaimed—not the invisible brother, not the guilty one, just himself.

chapters.title: A Letter That Gets Sent
chapters.summary: Mirabel writes to June—not a postcard but a letter, full sentences, his name signed plainly—and mails it to a real address. They begin a correspondence about the man they both lost. POV: Mirabel. Beat: resolution; truth chosen over the comfort of silence.

chapters.title: Blue Hour
chapters.summary: A year later, at dusk, Mirabel visits the lot where a small garden now grows, planted with Adaeze. He mails one final postcard—to himself—containing the sentence he spent twelve years practicing. POV: Mirabel, closing outward briefly to Ruth reading a news item about a song finally credited. Beat: peace earned, not granted.
